prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

In Ocean's wide domains, Half buried in the sands, Lie skeletons in chains, With shackled feet and hands. Beyond the fall of dews, Deeper than plummet lies, Float ships, with all their crews, No more to sink nor rise. There the black Slave-ship swims, Freighted with human forms, Whose fettered, fleshless limbs Are not the sport of storms. These are the bones of Slaves; They gleam from the abyss; They cry, from yawning waves, "We are the Witnesses!" Within Earth's wide domains Are markets for men's lives; Their necks are galled with chains, Their wrists are cramped with gyves. Dead bodies, that the kite In deserts makes its prey; Murders, that with affright Scare school-boys from their play! All evil thoughts and deeds; Anger, and lust, and pride; The foulest, rankest weeds, That choke Life's groaning tide! These are the woes of Slaves; They glare from the abyss; They cry, from unknown graves, "We are the Witnesses!"

Below are two polished options that preserve every detail, fact, and piece of imagery from the original text.

### Option 1: Professional & Eloquent Prose
*Best suited for speeches, essays, formal presentations, or historical commentary.*

> Across the vast expanse of the ocean, partially submerged beneath the sands, lie chained skeletons with shackled hands and feet. Far deeper than any soundings can measure, beyond the reach of falling dew, sunken vessels remain suspended with their entire crews—forever motionless in the depths. Among them drifts the dark slave ship, laden with human cargo whose bound, fleshless remains are no longer subject to the fury of ocean storms. These are the bones of the enslaved; they gleam from the oceanic abyss and cry out from the surging waves: *"We are the Witnesses!"*
>
> Likewise, across the land, human lives are bought and sold in open markets. Necks are chafed raw by heavy iron collar chains, and wrists are constricted by shackles. Deserts hold the unburied dead, preyed upon by kites, while acts of murder strike terror into schoolboys at play. Evil thoughts and deeds—anger, lust, and pride—act as the foulest, rankest weeds, suffocating the groaning tide of human existence. These are the profound agonies of the enslaved; they glare from the depths of oblivion and cry out from unmarked graves: *"We are the Witnesses!"*

---

### Option 2: Enhanced & Elevated Poetic Verse
*Best if you wish to retain the poetic rhythm and verse structure while enhancing its literary elegance.*

> Across the ocean’s vast domains,  
> Half-buried in the shifting sands,  
> Rest skeletal remains in chains,  
> With shackled feet and bounden hands.  
> Deeper than any plummet lies,  
> Far down beneath the falling dews,  
> Float silent ships that neither rise  
> Nor sink, entombed with all their crews.  
> 
> There drifts the slave-ship, dark and grim,  
> Heavy with captive human forms,  
> Whose fettered, pale, and fleshless limb  
> Is mocked no longer by the storms.  
> These are the bones of Slaves long lost;  
> They gleam within the deep abyss,  
> And cry above the waters tossed:  
> *"We are the Witnesses!"*  
> 
> Throughout the Earth’s expansive lands,  
> Men’s lives are bartered, bought, and sold;  
> Chafed necks are bound in iron bands,  
> And wrists the heavy shackles hold.  
> Unburied corpses, left to lie,  
> Become the desert scavenger's prey;  
> While dreadful deeds of murder high  
> Scare playing schoolboys from their play.  
> 
> All evil thoughts, all ruthless deeds—  
> Cruel anger, lust, and bitter pride—  
> Are like the rankest, foulest weeds  
> That choke life’s groaning, burdened tide.  
> These are the woes the enslaved possess;  
> They glare from out the deep abyss,  
> And cry from unknown graves’ recess:  
> *"We are the Witnesses!"*

outputs.L3:
**Voices from the Abyss: The Unyielding Witness of the Enslaved**

The transatlantic slave trade remains one of the darkest chapters in human history—a vast, institutionalized machinery of cruelty that left an indelible scar upon both the land and the sea. Across centuries, millions of innocent human beings were torn from their homelands, subjected to unimaginable suffering, and stripped of their basic rights. The true cost of this tragedy resides not only in historical archives, but in the very geography of our planet, preserved in silent, enduring monuments to lost life.

Deep beneath the waves of the Atlantic, far beyond the reach of human sight, lies a vast and tragic underwater cemetery. In the abyssal depths rest the chained skeletons of countless enslaved individuals who perished aboard slave ships during the harrowing journey of the Middle Passage. Lost to disease, starvation, or tossed overboard by ruthless traders, their iron-bound remains rest in the oceanic silent darkness. These submerged graves stand as eternal, incorruptible witnesses to the staggering human cost of the slave trade, preserving evidence of an era that sought to erase the very humanity of its victims.

Where the sea met the shore, the horror merely changed forms. On land, slave markets reduced precious human lives to mere economic commodities, displaying men, women, and children as goods to be bought, sold, and traded. Within this brutal terrestrial system, enslaved individuals were subjected to continuous physical bondage, horrific torture, and violent death. The soil of continents was soaked in the sweat and blood of those forced into labor, creating a landscape defined by systematic oppression and state-sanctioned violence.

Ultimately, the institution of slavery did not merely inflict physical destruction; it fueled a profound and pervasive moral corruption. To justify such atrocity, societies willingly poisoned their own consciences, replacing empathy with cold, calculating cruelty. This widespread evil produced a toxic culture of suffering that choked the essential spirit of human life, proving that a society built upon the subjugation of others inevitably decays from within.

Though centuries have passed, the legacy of this tragedy remains active in our collective memory. From the depths of the ocean floor to the uncounted, unmarked graves scattered across the land, the victims of this dark era cannot be silenced. Their resting places continuously cry out from the abyss, bearing unyielding witness against the atrocities committed against them—a permanent call to remembrance, justice, and the preservation of human dignity.

### The Silent Indictment: Witnesses of the Abyss

History often attempts to bury its darkest transgressions beneath the quiet passage of time, yet certain horrors leave an indelible mark upon the geography of the Earth and the soul of humanity. Among the most profound of these atrocities is the transatlantic slave trade and the institution of chattel slavery—a monstrous engine of greed that reshaped world empires at the cost of millions of lives. Through a haunting tapestry of visual agony, the human cost of this legacy is laid bare, spanning the suffocating depths of the Atlantic Ocean to the dust-choked, sun-scorched slave markets of the Americas. In these places, the fallen do not merely fade into history; they endure as eternal Witnesses, casting an inescapable moral indictment against systemic oppression and human cruelty.

The tragedy begins in the vast, indifferent expanse of the ocean. Beneath the rolling waves of the Middle Passage lies an unrecorded cemetery. Here, in the sunless depths of the abyss, rest the fettered skeletons of men, women, and children who perished aboard the slave ships. Iron manacles, oxidized by centuries of salt and water, still bind bone to bone upon the ocean floor. These submerged remains are the silent relics of a massive, cold-blooded violence—victims tossed overboard like ruined cargo, or who chose the mercy of the sea over the horror of the hold. Coral and current may envelop them, but time cannot erase their presence. The ocean itself becomes a cathedral of loss, holding fast to the evidence of a boundless catastrophe that human history tried to cast away.

Upon the land, the terror assumed a different, equally grueling form. In the bustling markets of colonial ports and plantation towns, human beings were dragged into the public eye to be appraised, priced, and sold as chattel. The text paints a harrowing picture of these market blocks: families torn apart in broad daylight, bodies branded with hot irons, and spirits battered under the unrelenting weight of physical and psychological torment. The earth where these captives bled—the cotton fields, the cane breaks, and the isolated plantation plots—holds millions of unmarked graves. These forgotten grounds serve as the terrestrial counterpart to the ocean floor, holding the physical traces of lives consumed by forced labor, brutal punishment, and deliberate dehumanization.

Yet, despite the perpetrators' attempts to erase the humanity of their victims, death does not grant the oppressors their desired silence. Transcending their tragic fates, these suffering souls emerge as an immortal vanguard: the "Witnesses." Crying out from the oceanic depths and from the quiet, nameless graves carved into the earth, their presence transforms the physical world into an active courtroom. Their cry is not one of physical sound, but of a deafening moral resonance that vibrates across generations. They stand in perpetual judgment over the systems that commodified their breath and the human cruelty that enabled such unimaginable malice.

Ultimately, this silent legacy acts as an inescapable mirror held up to human history. It forces every subsequent generation to confront the depths to which humanity can sink when greed and systemic hatred are institutionalized. The fettered skeletons in the abyss and the buried captives in the earth cannot be quieted by revisionist histories or the passage of centuries. Their persistent, ghostly testimony serves as an eternal warning and a solemn duty: to remember the atrocities of the past, to honor the humanity of those who suffered, and to relentlessly dismantle the enduring structures of tyranny and oppression wherever they remain.
outputs.L5:
The **ocean** has a way of stripping human beings down to their barest truths. Standing at the edge of the tide, where the cold, churning water licks at bare ankles, there is nowhere left to hide. The vast, indifferent expanse doesn't care for quiet excuses or carefully constructed facades; it only understands depth, momentum, and reality.

For years, I carried what you gave me—a beautiful, fragile **lie**. It was whispered under a grey autumn sky, spun so gently that it felt like comfort rather than deception. You told me we had time, that the distance between us was temporary, and that the future was something we could build together. I swallowed it whole, using your words as an anchor to keep from drifting. 

It took the unrelenting rhythm of the waves to make me realize I was holding onto a ghost. A lie, no matter how sweetly told, leaves you suspended in a shadow land. Because I believed it, I gave you my whole heart, only to receive **half** of yours in return. I was living a half-life, suspended in the twilight of partial truths, loving a person who only existed in the space between what you said and what you actually meant. You kept the other half of yourself guarded, buried deep like a forgotten shipwreck resting in the dark, abyssal plain.

Now, watching the foam retreat back into the great blue abyss, the weight finally shifts. The ocean teaches us that nothing stays buried forever; the tide always demands an accounting. I leave the lie here, on the wet sand, for the salt and surf to break apart into harmless grains. As the water pulls away, it carries the illusion with it, leaving me on the shore—no longer fractured, and finally ready to claim the whole of my own life.

counterfactuals.output:
Here is the text of Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's poem **"The Witnesses,"** published in his 1842 collection *Poems on Slavery*:

***

### **The Witnesses**

In Ocean's wide domains,
Half-buried in the sands,
Lie skeletons in chains,
With shackled feet and hands.

Beyond the fall of dews,
Deeper than plummet lies,
Float ships with all their crews,
No more to sink or rise.

There the huge sea-monster wastes
His strength, to make commotion;
And the shark, the shadow-caster,
Glides through the waste of Ocean.

There lie the bones of Slaves,
All day, all night, the same;
A cry among the waves,
That whispers of their shame.

These are the Witnesses,
These are the silent hosts;
This is the Skeleton Coast,
Where all the ships are ghosts.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a powerful 19th-century style abolitionist poem about the victims of the transatlantic slave trade lost at sea and on land.
counterfactuals.output:
O deep Atlantic, broad and dark,
Hide not the pathway of the bark!
Beneath thy cold, unmeasured wave,
Ten thousand souls have found a grave.
No stone marks where the captive lies,
Beneath the storm-unpitying skies;
Uncoffined, unlamented thrown,
Where abyssal currents mourn alone.

There iron bound the living fast
To dead men rotting at the mast,
Till sickness, grief, or ocean’s dread
Relieved the living from the dead.
The greedy shark pursued the trail,
Following the slaver's blood-stained sail,
To claim the harvest cast away
Before the dawning of the day.

Yet mourn not those alone who sleep
Deep in the silence of the deep—
For fiercer storms and darker waves
Awaited those made living slaves!
Whose feet were chained to foreign strands,
To bleed upon the tyrant’s lands.

Upon the scorched and weary plain,
Through fields of sugar and of cane,
Their bitter sweat enriched the soil,
In unrequited, hopeless toil.
The driver's lash, the heavy chain,
The mother's shriek of rending pain,
When from her breast her child was torn,
To bear the yoke that she had borne!

In silent night, the cotton row
Beheld a grief no tongue can know;
The soil was watered by their tears,
Through agonizing, languished years,
Till under sod, without a name,
They died within a nation's shame.

Think ye the God who rules the height
Beholds unmoved this awful night?
Think ye the ocean shall retain
The blood of millions who were slain?
Nay! From the deep floor to the sod,
That silent blood cries out to God!

Break down the scourge! Unbind the chain!
Let mercy wash the crimson stain!
For Earth and Sea at last shall yield
The secrets of the wave and field,
And Judgment claim the cruel trade,
When all the lost are whole again made.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you share a famous American Romantic poem that addresses the horrors of slavery using imagery of ocean depths and tragic ocean voyages?
counterfactuals.output:
A famous American Romantic poem that perfectly fits this description is **"The Slave-Ships"** (1834) by **John Greenleaf Whittier**. 

Whittier was one of the prominent "Fireside Poets" of the American Romantic movement and a passionate abolitionist. The poem was inspired by a horrific historical event aboard the French slave ship *Le Rôdeur* in 1819, where an outbreak of ophthalmia (a blinding eye infection) struck both the crew and the captive Africans. To claim insurance money, the captain ordered dozens of blinded, enslaved people to be thrown overboard into the Atlantic Ocean.

Whittier uses vivid, sublime, and tragic ocean imagery—raging storms, deep sea graves, and prowling sharks—to expose the unspeakable cruelty of the Middle Passage.

Here are key excerpts from the poem:

***

### **The Slave-Ships**
*By John Greenleaf Whittier (1834)*

"All ready?" selection made,
The dark-browed captain cried;
"Fall back, fall back, ye shivering shade,
And let the sea-wave hide!"
...

Up from the moonless ocean-floor
The silent phantoms rise,
And gaze upon the ship once more
With cold and sightless eyes!

They come from ocean's deepest bed,
Where rolling billows sweep,
To tell of horrors dark and dread,
Wrought on the stormy deep.

...

"Hark! from the ship's dark hold out-broke
A wild and despairing cry;
'Twas the voice of woman's agony,
Ere she was left to die!

And down, down through the ocean blue,
Slow sinking in the sea,
She went to her dark resting-place,
Where the ocean-monsters be."

...

"Overhead the storm-cloud lowers,
Darkness on the waters lies,
While beneath, the angry ocean
Yields its human sacrifice."

***

### **Why this poem fits the American Romantic era:**

1. **The Sublime and Terrifying Ocean:** Romantic literature often viewed nature—especially the ocean—as a vast, unstoppable, and awe-inspiring force. Whittier transforms the ocean into a massive, mournful graveyard ("ocean's deepest bed") that holds the secret horrors of the slave trade.
2. **Moral Outrage and Emotion:** Rather than presenting an abstract political argument, Whittier uses intense emotional realism—ghostly phantoms, cries from the hold, and the grim reality of drowning—to evoke deep empathy and moral dread in the reader.
3. **Haunting Imagery:** The imagery of sightless corpses floating up from the "moonless ocean-floor" mirrors the spiritual blindness of the slave traders, using the ocean depths as a metaphor for both physical death and moral depravity.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me an abolitionist poem about the Middle Passage and the evils of slavery.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Wake of Iron and Salt**

They dragged the sunshine from the coast,
And bound the night in iron bands,
Transforming living men to ghosts
Unmoored from home and native lands.
The wooden hull, a floating tomb,
Swayed heavy on the surging tide,
And carried in its stifling womb
The souls that lived, the souls that died.

Deep in the dark, where shadows weep,
Stacked soul to soul and breath to breath,
They lay in agony asleep,
Or whispered prayers for early death.
No light to grace the endless gloom,
No balm to soothe the rusted chain;
The air was thick with fever’s bloom,
And every timbers groaned with pain.

The grey Atlantic knows the tale—
It remembers every stifled cry,
The mothers lost beneath the sail,
The tears that salted sea and sky.
Behind the ship, the sleek sharks swam,
A quiet fleet that knew the trade,
When sickened flesh, ignored by man,
Was to the hungry waters weighed.

Oh, tell us not of civilized grace,
Nor speak of merchant’s honest gain,
When built upon a stolen race
And nurtured by the lash and chain!
To tear the child from mother’s breast,
To price a spirit, brand the skin,
To call a land by freedom blessed
While steeped in this unholy sin!

How long shall heaven bear the sight?
How long shall Earth absorb the blood?
Awake, O world! Stand for the right,
And sweep away this guilty flood!
Rend every shackle, break the rod,
Let every ocean scream its shame,
Until the stolen sons of God
Are free in justice’ holy name!
